title: Rigorously Certified Neural-Network Computation of Nonlinear Water Waves at Near-Machine Precision
authors: Michal Shavit, Yongji Wang, Tristan Buckmaster
abstract: We present a computational framework that combines machine-learning-based discovery with rigorous computer-assisted numerical certification and formal verification for strongly nonlinear partial differential equations. We demonstrate the approach for periodic gravity-capillary traveling water waves. Physics-informed neural networks are used as a search mechanism, with the wave profile, wave speed and, in continuation experiments, surface tension learned directly from the governing equations without training data. Through a staged training and refinement procedure, the neural networks achieve near-machine-precision residuals of the governing equations, even in strongly nonlinear regimes. A single formulation recovers high-amplitude Stokes waves, Crapper waves and Wilton ripples. Continuation from a high-amplitude Wilton ripple in surface tension reveals new high-amplitude candidate solutions. We freeze one candidate as an explicit finite representation and rigorously certify a uniform bound on its governing-equation residual using interval arithmetic, accounting for floating-point roundoff, Fourier truncation, aliasing and grid-to-continuum errors. This independently validates the neural-network accuracy. We formalize the certification argument in Lean, which machine-checks the deductions from certified numerical bounds to the residual theorem. Both the interval certification and formalization were developed with substantial assistance from a large language model, while the validity of the result remains independent of the language model: the numerical bounds are rigorously enclosed by interval arithmetic and the subsequent mathematical deductions are checked by the Lean kernel. Together, these steps provide a pipeline from neural discovery to rigorous numerical certification and machine-checked verification with auditable mathematical guarantees.

infographic.key_insight: Neural networks discover strongly nonlinear water-wave candidates with near-machine-precision equation residuals, while interval arithmetic and Lean independently certify a residual bound for one candidate.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework shows how learned PDE solutions can gain auditable numerical guarantees rather than relying solely on sampled residuals.
method: Train physics-informed neural networks without training data to learn wave profiles, speeds and continuation parameters.
Freeze one candidate into a finite representation and bound its residual using interval arithmetic, including roundoff, truncation, aliasing and grid-to-continuum errors.
Use Lean to machine-check the deductions from certified numerical bounds to the residual theorem.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports recovery of Stokes waves, Crapper waves and Wilton ripples, new high-amplitude candidates through continuation, and rigorous residual certification of one candidate.
infographic.watch_item: A certified small residual is not by itself a proof of existence, uniqueness or stability of a nearby exact wave.
infographic.paper_title: Rigorously Certified Neural-Network Computation of Nonlinear Water Waves at Near-Machine Precision

title: SwarmEvolve: Latent Agent Swarms for Evolutionary Discovery and Optimization
authors: Qile Jiang, George Em Karniadakis
abstract: LLM-guided evolutionary search uses AI agents to improve programs for mathematical and computational problems by iteratively refining solutions and combining high-scoring methods. However, the process is often slow because the LLM generates a long textual chain of thought for each round and must repeat this generation many times to maintain population diversity. We present SwarmEvolve, a framework in which hundreds of low-cost agents per round work in swarms, reason in latent space without decoding to text, and share information by passing KV caches. Each swarm studies the problem from a different angle. A novelty filter keeps the most distinct agent ideas by directly measuring the distances between the agents' hidden state vectors. Crossover of ideas happens naturally in latent space, as a summarizer agent receives the combined KV caches of all swarm members. On 21 problems in mathematical discovery and scientific computing, SwarmEvolve gets the highest average score and needs a median of only 3 to 8 minutes to reach the best scores that other state-of-the-art frameworks reach in 60 minutes. On several problems, SwarmEvolve with Qwen3 8B improves on the solutions that AlphaEvolve first found with frontier LLMs. Our work shows that agent swarms that communicate in latent space offer a fast, low-cost approach to program search for scientific problems.

infographic.key_insight: SwarmEvolve accelerates evolutionary program search by letting hundreds of agents reason and exchange ideas in latent space rather than generating textual reasoning.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Latent-space coordination offers a potentially faster, lower-cost way to optimize programs for mathematical discovery and scientific computing.
method: Run low-cost agent swarms that explore different approaches and communicate through KV caches.
Select distinct ideas using distances between agents’ hidden-state vectors.
Combine swarm members’ KV caches in a summarizer agent to perform latent-space crossover.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 21 problems, SwarmEvolve reports the highest average score and median times of 3–8 minutes to match best scores reached by competing frameworks in 60 minutes.
infographic.watch_item: KV-cache sharing requires access to model internals, which may limit deployment through standard hosted-model APIs.
infographic.paper_title: SwarmEvolve: Latent Agent Swarms for Evolutionary Discovery and Optimization

title: EvoOPD: Evolving Privileged Information Strategies for Black-Box On-Policy Distillation
authors: Ximo Zhu, Ruiqi Liu, Yi Han, Zhengan Wu, Gengsheng Li, ZiAn Wang
abstract: Proprietary language models exhibit strong reasoning and coding capabilities, but their output distributions are inaccessible, making fine-grained distillation methods that rely on teacher logits difficult to apply directly to black-box models. We observe that rich textual feedback from a black-box teacher can be treated as privileged information (PI) and converted, through a PI-conditioned privileged teacher, into dense supervision signals on the student's own trajectories. However, what PI should be acquired from the teacher to most effectively support student learning remains unclear. PI strategies that differ in where they focus, what information they request, and how much detail they provide can have substantially different effects on the current student, and their relative effectiveness can further change as training progresses. Based on this observation, we propose Evolving Privileged Information Strategies for Black-Box On-Policy Distillation (EvoOPD), which treats PI acquisition itself as an optimization problem and maintains a PI Strategy Bank that evolves with the student state. EvoOPD uses the measured repair utility of PI on the current student to adapt the focus, information type, and granularity of teacher feedback, allowing the acquired information to continually match the student's learning needs. We systematically evaluate EvoOPD on mathematical reasoning and code generation with Qwen3-1.7B, 4B, and 8B students. EvoOPD achieves the best overall performance in all six model-task settings, improving over the strongest baseline in each setting by an average of 2.14 percentage points in mathematics and 1.30 points in code. Further analysis shows that the relative effectiveness of PI acquisition strategies changes with student state, making a fixed strategy difficult to sustain as the best choice throughout distillation.

infographic.key_insight: EvoOPD improves black-box distillation by evolving teacher-feedback strategies to match the student's changing learning needs.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It enables dense supervision from proprietary models without access to their logits by routing textual feedback through a privileged-information-conditioned teacher.
method: Acquire textual feedback as privileged information on student-generated trajectories.
Convert that feedback into dense supervision using a privileged teacher.
Evolve a strategy bank using measured repair utility to adapt feedback focus, type, and granularity.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across mathematics and code generation with Qwen3-1.7B, 4B, and 8B students, EvoOPD leads all six model-task settings, averaging gains over each setting's strongest baseline of 2.14 percentage points in math and 1.30 points in code.
infographic.watch_item: Teacher-query costs and strategy-evaluation overhead are not quantified in the abstract, leaving practical efficiency unclear.
infographic.paper_title: EvoOPD: Evolving Privileged Information Strategies for Black-Box On-Policy Distillation

title: On the Generalization Limitation of On-Policy Distillation for Post-RL Consolidation
authors: Yichen Wang, Yufa Zhou, Siqi Zhu, Haozheng Luo, Jingzhi Bao, Zhichao Liu
abstract: Multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) extends on-policy distillation (OPD) to consolidate capabilities from multiple teachers. Although prior work reports near-perfect in-distribution (IND) distillation performance, we find that this can mask incomplete capability consolidation beyond the supervised distribution. A preliminary study on synthetic reasoning shows that OPD does not fully transfer teachers' generalization capabilities. We then extend this investigation to real-world tasks, evaluating extrapolative and compositional generalization across mathematical reasoning, coding, agent, and long-context capabilities using Qwen3 models. Across extrapolative settings, OPD and MOPD reach 96.04-102.73% of their teachers' IND scores. Yet their out-of-distribution (OOD) scores remain 2.45-16.25% below the base model's. Across three compositional settings, MOPD improves IND performance over the base model, but its performance on composed tasks as OOD remains 18.19-24.34% below that of the best teachers. To understand these gaps, we examine teacher capability and data coverage as two potential bottlenecks. Jointly alleviating these bottlenecks eliminates OOD forgetting in our experiments and suggests the potential for generalization beyond the teacher. (M)OPD also reduces OOD forgetting on average relative to its reinforcement learning (RL) baselines. Analysis of the associated update geometry reveals smaller and more spectrally concentrated updates on average than those of the RL baselines, along with greater shared update structure under MOPD. Motivated by these findings, we propose geometry-based patching and base-preserving replay to improve OOD performance while largely preserving IND performance. Our findings identify a blind spot in capability consolidation via (M)OPD, highlighting the need for algorithms that explicitly support OOD retention and generalization.

infographic.key_insight: Near-teacher performance on supervised distributions can mask incomplete capability transfer and out-of-distribution forgetting after on-policy distillation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Teams consolidating specialized models should test extrapolative and compositional generalization rather than relying on in-distribution scores alone.
method: Evaluate single- and multi-teacher on-policy distillation on synthetic reasoning and Qwen3-based tasks.
Probe teacher capability, data coverage, and update geometry as explanations for generalization gaps.
Propose geometry-based patching and base-preserving replay to improve OOD retention.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across math, coding, agent, and long-context evaluations, extrapolative IND scores reached 96.04–102.73% of teacher scores, while OOD scores remained 2.45–16.25% below the base model; compositional OOD scores were 18.19–24.34% below the best teachers.
infographic.watch_item: Eliminating OOD forgetting by jointly improving teacher capability and data coverage was demonstrated only in the reported experiments, not as a general guarantee.
infographic.paper_title: On the Generalization Limitation of On-Policy Distillation for Post-RL Consolidation

title: Constructive Probability, Foundations and Numerical Analysis for mathematical finance and machine learning
authors: Claudio Albanese
abstract: This monograph sets out a constructive theory of stochastic processes in the continuum, in the sense of constructive field theory: the continuum is not postulated but reached as the limit of a sequence of lattice approximations, with the renormalisation the limit requires exhibited rather than assumed, and the limit controlled by estimates that can be checked. The primitive object is not a sigma-algebra but de Finetti's prevision, the price of finitely many gambles at a fixed resolution, which coherence turns into a conditional expectation. The theorem at the centre of the book, called plainly the fundamental theorem, is at once de Finetti's fundamental theorem of probability, the fundamental theorem of Bayesian statistics, and the one-period fundamental theorem of asset pricing; the financial vocabulary is a convenience only. The applications are two, mathematical finance and machine learning, and they are one mathematics read in opposite directions: an assessment is a price in the one and a prediction in the other, and both are computed by one adjoint recursion, the adjoint of a propagation in the first case and backpropagation in the second. Carried through, the two directions give sharp rates of convergence rather than asymptotic orders: for the moments of Ito diffusions, for the value function of Feynman-Kac semigroups, and for the measure changes of the fundamental theorem, the last as a limit theorem for reweighted generators, under a condition keeping the reweighting well behaved. A measure change is thus calculated, not postulated: a lattice approximation with Farkas' lemma computes it, completeness makes it unique, and the passage to the continuum is earned by the regularity of what is computed. Sixty-seven Python scripts regenerate every numerical table, and much of the finite-dimensional core of the argument has been verified in Lean 4.

infographic.key_insight: Coherent finite-resolution prices or predictions provide a constructive foundation for stochastic processes, connecting Bayesian inference and asset pricing through controlled lattice-to-continuum limits.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework connects financial valuation and machine-learning prediction through adjoint recursions while providing quantitative convergence guarantees for stochastic computations.
method: Start with coherent previsions on finite lattices to construct conditional expectations.
Refine lattices toward the continuum, explicitly tracking renormalisation and convergence estimates.
Compute measure changes using Farkas’ lemma and connect pricing and prediction through adjoint recursions.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports sharp convergence rates, 67 Python scripts regenerating every numerical table, and Lean 4 verification of much of the finite-dimensional core.
infographic.watch_item: Continuum measure-change guarantees depend on regularity and well-behaved reweighting; the abstract does not establish scalability for large machine-learning systems.
infographic.paper_title: Constructive Probability, Foundations and Numerical Analysis for mathematical finance and machine learning

title: Extending graph metrics to hyperspaces of vertex sets: optimization and reinforcement learning applications
authors: Natalia Jonard-Pérez, Enrique A. Sánchez-Pérez, Sergi Sanjuan
abstract: An undirected connected graph can be interpreted as a metric space by considering the path distance between its vertices. Extending this perspective, we explore how walks in the graph, viewed as sequences of subsets of vertices $V$, fit into a more general framework where the path distance emerges as a special case of broader metrics that define hypertopologies on the space of subsets of $V$. In this paper, we propose a general framework to address this issue, motivated by the extension of recent reinforcement learning algorithms on graphs through Lipschitz function extensions. Our approach demonstrates how models for dynamical systems and related machine learning techniques can be adapted to (quasi-pseudo-metric) hyperspaces, offering a novel perspective for the analysis and modeling of dynamical systems. Finally, we illustrate the practical relevance of our theoretical contributions through a concrete graph optimization example, highlighting the utility and effectiveness of our proposed approach.

infographic.key_insight: Graph path distance extends to metrics on vertex subsets, providing a framework for modeling set-valued walks and dynamical systems.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework could extend graph-based reinforcement learning and optimization to states represented by vertex sets rather than individual vertices.
method: Treat a connected undirected graph as a metric space using path distance.
Define broader quasi-pseudo-metric structures on vertex subsets that induce hyperspace topologies.
Use Lipschitz function extensions to connect hyperspace models with graph-based reinforcement learning.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports a concrete graph optimization example but provides no datasets, benchmarks, or quantitative performance results.
infographic.watch_item: Practical scalability needs evaluation because the number of possible vertex subsets grows exponentially with graph size.
infographic.paper_title: Extending graph metrics to hyperspaces of vertex sets: optimization and reinforcement learning applications

title: Self-Privileged Fine-Tuning
authors: Yangrong Hu, Xueyu Zhou, Yue Wu, Jian Huang
abstract: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) is a key component of language model post-training, enabling effective task adaptation and serving as an important foundation for subsequent reinforcement learning. Recent methods seek to improve SFT by introducing token-level weights into the training objective, where these weights are typically derived from a model's output distribution at each token position. To better understand how such weighting schemes affect SFT, we analyze their optimization objectives and theoretically characterize the target distributions they induce. Our analysis shows that dynamic weighting methods, such as Dynamic Fine-Tuning (DFT), induce a heavily sharpened distribution, whereas static weighting methods fit a target distribution proportional to the product of the data distribution and a frozen prior. These findings suggest that static weighting provides a more stable training target, while its effectiveness critically depends on the quality of the prior distribution. Building on this observation, we propose Self-Privileged Fine-Tuning (SPFT), which uses a frozen copy of the initial model conditioned on privileged information (such as ground truth for mathematical questions) as a prior to provide guidance for token-level weighting during fine-tuning. Through a Bayesian decomposition, we further show that SPFT reweights the standard static prior according to how informative each target token is for predicting the ground-truth outcome, thereby assigning larger weights to more predictive tokens. Experiments on mathematical reasoning and code generation show that SPFT improves over standard SFT and other baselines across the main settings.

infographic.key_insight: Self-Privileged Fine-Tuning (SPFT) weights training tokens using a frozen initial model given privileged information, emphasizing tokens that are more predictive of the correct outcome.
infographic.engineering_relevance: SPFT offers a token-weighted supervised fine-tuning approach for improving mathematical reasoning and code generation.
method: Analyze induced targets: dynamic weighting heavily sharpens distributions, while static weighting combines the data distribution with a frozen prior.
Use a frozen initial model conditioned on privileged information, such as ground-truth answers, to generate token-level weights.
Apply these weights during fine-tuning; a Bayesian decomposition links the weighting to tokens' predictive value for the outcome.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports improvements over standard SFT and other baselines across the main mathematical reasoning and code generation settings, without specifying benchmarks or effect sizes.
infographic.watch_item: Effectiveness depends on the quality of the privileged prior, and implementation requires generating token-level weights with a frozen model.
infographic.paper_title: Self-Privileged Fine-Tuning

title: Improving Hydrofoil Efficiency Through Simulation-Driven Design Optimization
authors: Ante Sikirica, Ivana Lučin, Marta Alvir, Tin Matulja
abstract: Foil windsurfing is a sport in which competitors fine-tune their setup to optimize performance under varying environmental conditions. However, such adjustments are typically guided by intuition. This paper presents a methodology for improving hydrofoil design using computational fluid dynamics. First, structured light scanning was used to obtain the geometry of a conventional hydrofoil. Subsequently, five derived designs have been explored, inspired by advancements in airplane wing design. Following this, a preliminary design was selected, and a design of experiments approach was implemented. Generated simulation data were used to train a machine learning surrogate, which is ultimately used in the multi-objective design optimization. While the surrogate-based approach yielded promising results, it was limited to exploring a restricted set of design parameters. To overcome this constraint, additional improvements were attained through adjoint optimization, demonstrating that comparable performance can be achieved with a distinctly different hydrofoil design. Finally, the conventional design was refined through adjoint optimization. Notably, adjoint optimization yielded a 15% increase in efficiency. The results suggest that both proposed approaches can produce novel hydrofoil designs capable of outperforming the original configuration under specific conditions; however, due to its inherent flexibility, the adjoint approach with realistic constraints offers more freedom in the design exploration process.

infographic.key_insight: Simulation-driven optimization improved hydrofoil efficiency, with adjoint optimization delivering a reported 15% increase over the conventional design.
infographic.engineering_relevance: CFD-based design optimization can replace intuition-led hydrofoil tuning with systematic exploration of higher-performing geometries.
method: Digitize a conventional hydrofoil using structured-light scanning and explore five aircraft-wing-inspired designs.
Use design-of-experiments CFD data to train a machine-learning surrogate for multi-objective optimization.
Apply adjoint optimization to refine geometries beyond the surrogate’s restricted design parameters.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports promising surrogate-based results and a 15% efficiency increase from adjoint optimization, with gains tied to specific operating conditions.
infographic.watch_item: Benefits require validation across operating conditions; surrogate parameter limits and realistic geometric constraints affect design exploration.
infographic.paper_title: Improving Hydrofoil Efficiency Through Simulation-Driven Design Optimization

title: Dynamic Optimistic Constrained OCO with Memory via Delay Equivalence
authors: Mohammed Abdullah, George Iosifidis, Salah Eddine Elayoubi, Tijani Chahed
abstract: Online Convex Optimization with memory and time-varying constraints (COCO-M) is a recently-introduced framework that captures the dynamics of stateful online learning and non-stochastic control with budget constraints. Despite its expressive power, COCO-M remains largely understudied. In this work, we tackle this problem in its full scale, providing an optimistic algorithm that incorporates untrusted predictions to tame universal dynamic regret and cumulative constraint violation. Our analysis leverages a potent reduction from memory to delay and treats state-dependent gradients as delayed feedback. We establish the first bounds that adapt to both environment non-stationarity (path length $P_T$) and prediction accuracy, while lifting previous restrictive assumptions such as functional separability. En route to these results, we derive findings of independent interest for the memory-to-delay reduction, and for delayed OCO with time-varying constraints. The proposed framework ensures sublinear worst-case guarantees that improve with prediction accuracy, reaching $\mathcal O(1)$ regret under perfect predictions, with cumulative constraint violation (CCV) $\mathcal O(\sqrt{T})$ for unknown $P_T$ and $\mathcal O(\log T)$ for known or online observable $P_T$ , while recovering the optimal COCO rates when memory disappears.

infographic.key_insight: Reducing memory to delayed feedback enables optimistic constrained online learning with guarantees that adapt to environment changes and prediction accuracy.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework supports stateful online learning and non-stochastic control under time-varying budget constraints, using predictions without requiring them to be reliable.
method: Reduce memory effects to delay and treat state-dependent gradients as delayed feedback.
Incorporate untrusted predictions into an optimistic constrained online optimization algorithm.
Adapt dynamic regret and cumulative constraint violation bounds to path length and prediction accuracy.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical guarantees, not empirical evaluation: perfect predictions yield O(1) regret, with cumulative constraint violation O(√T) for unknown path length or O(log T) when path length is known or online observable.
infographic.watch_item: The strongest constraint-violation guarantee requires known or online-observable path length, which may be unavailable in deployment.
infographic.paper_title: Dynamic Optimistic Constrained OCO with Memory via Delay Equivalence

title: Data-driven discovery of intrinsic Lie point symmetries of differential equation systems
authors: Ilker Gurcan, Kadir Ustun, Ramazan Gokberk Cinbis
abstract: Discovering continuous symmetries directly from differential-equation data can reveal geometric structure for model reduction and scientific machine learning without symbolic determining equations or a closed-form representation of the governing system. We formulate intrinsic Lie point-symmetry discovery as an operator-theoretic problem on sampled jet-space data. Admissible generators are identified from a sampled determining operator and separated from redundant, solution-dependent, and geometrically trivial directions. The framework combines prolongation, sequential subspace restrictions, and a fixed nonlinear dictionary linear in trainable coefficients. A rank-stabilization preflight test diagnoses systems whose represented intrinsic symmetry algebra does not stabilize under dictionary refinement. On a controlled differential-equation benchmark with an analytically known 11-dimensional represented intrinsic symmetry algebra, the method recovers the complete represented generator set, reproduces its Lie-bracket structure to numerical precision, and approximates a known generator beyond the training domain. Here we show that explicit intrinsic continuous-symmetry generators can be recovered from data obtained from exact or approximate differential systems.

infographic.key_insight: Intrinsic Lie point-symmetry generators can be recovered directly from sampled differential-equation data without symbolic determining equations or closed-form governing equations.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Recovered symmetries can reveal geometric structure useful for model reduction and scientific machine learning.
method: Build a sampled determining operator on jet-space data using prolongation.
Apply sequential subspace restrictions to separate intrinsic generators from redundant, solution-dependent, and geometrically trivial directions.
Fit a fixed nonlinear dictionary linear in trainable coefficients, with a rank-stabilization preflight test under dictionary refinement.
infographic.evidence_signal: On a controlled benchmark with a known 11-dimensional represented intrinsic symmetry algebra, the method recovered all represented generators, reproduced their Lie brackets to numerical precision, and approximated a known generator beyond the training domain.
infographic.watch_item: Recovery is limited by the chosen dictionary's expressivity; the preflight test flags cases where the represented symmetry algebra fails to stabilize under refinement.
infographic.paper_title: Data-driven discovery of intrinsic Lie point symmetries of differential equation systems

title: Adversarial Training with Large Step Sizes: Implicit Bias, Optimization, and Sharpness
authors: Yi Feng, Andrea Paudice
abstract: Adversarial Training (AT) is an important method for improving model robustness. We study the dynamics of deterministic Gradient Descent (GD) in AT. Most existing works in this direction focus on the small or vanishing step sizes regime, where GD resembles a continuous-time flow. However, such step sizes can make training inefficient and are rarely used in practice. In this paper, we study the AT dynamics of GD with large constant step sizes. We first study GD in adversarial linear logistic regression, focusing on two aspects: where the model parameters converge (implicit bias) and how quickly the losses decrease (optimization). We then turn to neural networks training and study how the sharpness of losses evolve during AT. Our results advance the understanding of the behaviors of GD with large step sizes in AT and highlight three key differences from its behavior in Standard Training (ST): (i) the implicit bias gap between AT and ST, previously established only for small step sizes, persists for arbitrarily large constant step sizes, (ii) different from ST, there is no uniform rate of convergence for the optimization error in AT, and (iii) sharpness can exhibit two-stage dynamics that differ from the Edge-of-Stability behavior observed in ST.

infographic.key_insight: With large constant gradient-descent steps, adversarial training differs from standard training in implicit bias, convergence rates, and sharpness dynamics.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Learning-rate choices for robust models should account for adversarial-training dynamics rather than assume standard-training convergence and stability behavior.
method: Study deterministic gradient descent with large constant step sizes.
Analyze implicit bias and loss convergence in adversarial linear logistic regression.
Investigate loss-sharpness evolution during adversarial neural-network training.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports an implicit-bias gap persisting for arbitrarily large constant steps, no uniform optimization-error convergence rate, and possible two-stage sharpness dynamics, but provides no datasets or numerical metrics.
infographic.watch_item: The analysis centers on deterministic gradient descent; applicability to stochastic optimizers and practical training pipelines requires validation.
infographic.paper_title: Adversarial Training with Large Step Sizes: Implicit Bias, Optimization, and Sharpness

title: Using Transformers for Teaching and Learning via Symbolic Distillation of Neural A-life Agents
authors: Shuwei Wang, Vadim Bulitko, Matthew R. G. Brown, Michael Youngblood, Ramon Lawrence, Roscoe Smith
abstract: Neural networks controlling behavior of A-life agents can evolve over multiple generations. While effective in making the agents survive, such networks are generally opaque to a human observer. Furthermore, the neural weights cannot be transferred between agents with different neural architectures. Distilling such neural networks into compact symbolic policies can help humans understand agent behavior in A-life. Additionally, it allows the agents to share their knowledge in a compact fashion, improving population-level learning. Distilling a neural policy into a symbolic policy is typically performed by searching the space of symbolic policies to find one that approximates the neural policy. However, even with a domain-specific language the space of policies can be large, necessitating incomplete stochastic search such as genetic algorithms. Yet the distillation remains computationally expensive. We propose to instead use a transformer pre-trained on readily available random percept-action data. Doing so speeds up distillation substantially. We derive the transformer architecture via a neural architecture search. Empirical results compare different distillation methods and the influence of the symbolic space on A-life population dynamics through self-reflection and teaching and learning.

infographic.key_insight: A pre-trained transformer accelerates conversion of opaque neural A-life policies into compact symbolic policies for human interpretation and agent-to-agent knowledge sharing.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Symbolic policies offer a compact way to transfer behavior across agents with different neural architectures without sharing incompatible neural weights.
method: Pre-train a transformer on readily available random percept-action data.
Select the transformer architecture through neural architecture search.
Distill neural policies into symbolic policies for self-reflection, teaching, and learning.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports substantially faster distillation and empirical comparisons of distillation methods and symbolic policy spaces, including their effects on A-life population dynamics, but gives no numerical results.
infographic.watch_item: Policy fidelity and transfer performance require validation for each symbolic language and agent environment.
infographic.paper_title: Using Transformers for Teaching and Learning via Symbolic Distillation of Neural A-life Agents

title: Asymptotic Optimality of $cμ$-Rule for LLM Inference Scheduling under Memory Constraint
authors: Zhenghao Li, Shengbo Wang, Nian Si
abstract: Large language model (LLM) inference, the process by which a pre-trained model receives an input prompt and generates output tokens sequentially, has become increasingly important with the widespread deployment of LLM-based applications. As inference workloads continue to scale, GPU memory has emerged as a critical bottleneck: the long input prompts and generation sequences common in agentic and reasoning workloads lead to substantial key-value (KV) cache usage. In this paper, we study the resulting online scheduling problem from a queueing perspective. Requests arrive stochastically with heterogeneous prompt and output lengths, undergo prefill and autoregressive decode, and compete for a finite KV-cache capacity. Unlike classical queueing models, the duration of a processing step depends on both prefill computation and KV-cache I/O, so service capacity is jointly determined by computation, memory access, and memory occupancy. We develop a fluid model that reduces the system to a multiclass single-server queue with effective service rates capturing computation, memory access, and memory capacity. This fluid analysis yields a $cμ$ priority rule, where the effective service rate $μ$ is jointly determined by computational speed, memory bandwidth, and memory capacity. We prove that this rule minimizes cumulative holding cost in the fluid model and, for a finite workload, also minimizes completion time and maximizes full-run output-token throughput. We then construct a feasible scheduling policy for the original finite system and prove that its scaled dynamics converge to the optimal fluid policy. Finally, experiments on a real LLM serving engine using an NVIDIA H800 show that practical implementations of the proposed priority rule substantially reduce average latency while maintaining high throughput relative to existing scheduling policies.

infographic.key_insight: A cμ priority rule that accounts for compute, memory bandwidth, and KV-cache capacity is optimal in the fluid model and asymptotically achievable in the finite system.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Memory-aware request prioritization can reduce LLM inference latency while preserving high throughput under limited GPU KV-cache capacity.
method: Reduce heterogeneous prefill and decode workloads to a multiclass fluid queue with effective service rates.
Prove cμ optimality for cumulative holding cost and, for finite workloads, completion time and full-run output-token throughput.
Construct a feasible finite-system policy whose scaled dynamics converge to the optimal fluid policy.
infographic.evidence_signal: Experiments on a real LLM serving engine using an NVIDIA H800 report substantially lower average latency while maintaining high throughput relative to existing scheduling policies.
infographic.watch_item: Optimality is fluid-model and asymptotic; finite-system performance depends on implementing priorities under actual compute, bandwidth, and KV-cache constraints.
infographic.paper_title: Asymptotic Optimality of $cμ$-Rule for LLM Inference Scheduling under Memory Constraint

title: Spectral and Subspace Dynamics of LoRA in Supervised Fine-Tuning and Reinforcement Learning
authors: Chenruo Liu, Zihan Wang, Yijun Dong, Qi Lei
abstract: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) is commonly used in both supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL), often under similar optimizer settings. Yet, how the different dynamics of the two stages manifest in the low-rank increment that LoRA optimizes remains unclear. Tracking the singular spectrum and subspaces of LoRA updates on mathematical reasoning tasks, we find that RL concentrates the spectrum at every learning rate, while SFT expands it at moderate learning rates; moreover, RL rotates the singular subspaces much faster than SFT at small learning rates. Interpolating between SFT and RL one ingredient at a time, we pinpoint group-mean baseline subtraction as the source of both contrasts. A quadratic multi-index model updated via LoRA unveils the underlying mechanism: group-mean baseline subtraction tilts the balance between two competing forces, coherent fitting and gradient noise, toward spectral concentration and faster subspace rotation, while forcing the risk-favorable learning rate to be low. Guided by these dynamics, we tailor LoRA updates to each stage: in SFT, we flatten the spectrum of the full update to spread adaptation across singular directions, whereas in RL, we flatten the part of the update outside the current LoRA increment span to promote subspace rotation. Experiments on mathematical reasoning tasks across multiple models show that the respective configurations for SFT and RL yield the best performance among the compared methods in most evaluated settings.

infographic.key_insight: LoRA dynamics differ by training stage: RL concentrates singular spectra and rotates subspaces faster at small learning rates, with group-mean baseline subtraction driving both contrasts with SFT.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Stage-specific LoRA updates may improve mathematical reasoning by spreading adaptation across singular directions in SFT and promoting subspace rotation in RL.
method: Track LoRA update spectra and singular subspaces during SFT and RL.
Isolate training ingredients and explain baseline subtraction effects using a quadratic multi-index model.
Flatten full-update spectra for SFT; flatten the component outside the current LoRA increment span for RL.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across multiple models on mathematical reasoning tasks, the respective SFT and RL configurations perform best among compared methods in most evaluated settings.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not quantify gains or computational overhead, and generalization beyond mathematical reasoning remains unestablished.
infographic.paper_title: Spectral and Subspace Dynamics of LoRA in Supervised Fine-Tuning and Reinforcement Learning

title: The Gold Rush in AI4Math, II: What are signatures of AI-assisted Proofs?
authors: Yuanchuan Guo, Jiashun Jin, Zheng Tracy Ke, Bingcheng Sui
abstract: The growing use of AI in mathematics raises a question: can we detect AI involvement in proofs, separately from AI assistance with writing? Historical arXiv papers, recent papers disclosing substantive AI use, and manuscripts released by OpenAI provide a rich empirical basis for studying this question. However, several challenges remain: lack of matched case-control pairs; potential incompleteness of disclosure; and lack of ready-to-use features designed to capture signals of AI involvement in proofs. To address these challenges, we construct five cohorts comprising 8,281 papers by combining existing manuscripts with those we produced using generative AI. These cohorts span different levels of AI involvement and include matched pairs of papers addressing the same research problems. We then introduce ProofTrace, a framework that represents each paper as a graph of immediate proof support (GIPS) and extracts interpretable features of mathematical organization. Our study yields three discoveries. First, principal-component projections of our features reveal a qualitative gradient of AI involvement, where AI-reworded papers remain close to human papers, the two AI-generated cohorts depart in broadly shared directions, and papers disclosing substantive AI use occupy intermediate positions which shifts toward AI-generated cohorts over time. Second, we identify recurring signatures of AI-generated proofs, such as fewer externally cited results, greater reliance on intermediate conclusions, and altered graph connectivity; many of these signatures persist under controls for research field, manuscript length, or graph size. Finally, in a separate detection experiment, ProofTrace distinguishes human-written papers from those disclosing substantive AI use. Its performance remains stable under AI rewording, whereas the performance of state-of-the-art text-based detectors declines sharply.

infographic.key_insight: ProofTrace reveals structural signatures of AI-generated proofs that differ from changes caused by AI rewording alone.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Graph-based analysis of proof organization could complement text-based detectors when assessing substantive AI involvement in mathematical papers.
method: Construct five cohorts totaling 8,281 papers, including matched papers addressing the same research problems.
Represent each paper as a graph of immediate proof support and extract interpretable structural features.
Analyze feature projections, test structural signatures under controls, and evaluate detection robustness to AI rewording.
infographic.evidence_signal: AI-generated proofs show fewer externally cited results, greater reliance on intermediate conclusions, and altered connectivity; detection of disclosed substantive AI use remains stable under AI rewording while text-based detector performance declines sharply.
infographic.watch_item: Potentially incomplete AI-use disclosures limit confidence in cohort labels and detection results.
infographic.paper_title: The Gold Rush in AI4Math, II: What are signatures of AI-assisted Proofs?

title: Randomized and Oracle-Based Feasible Directions Methods for Nonsmooth Nonconvex Constrained Optimization
authors: Dan Greenstein, Nadav Hallak
abstract: Minimizing nonsmooth nonconvex objectives over general convex sets using no derivatives of the objective, together with structural access to the constraint set, poses a fundamental geometric difficulty: at boundary points, the feasible direction cone may fail to be closed, preventing the construction of finite sets of search directions that capture all feasible descent directions. We develop a feasible-directions framework for problems structured as the difference between a continuously differentiable function and a convex function over a closed convex set, and access the objective without knowledge of its decomposition, through exact line searches along feasible segments. To address the geometric obstruction, we introduce $η$-feasible directions, which remain uniformly separated from the boundary of the feasible direction cone, enabling finite-direction search even in the presence of nonlinear constraints. We present two algorithmic realizations of this framework. The first assumes access to an $η$-direction oracle and extends feasible-directions methods from linear to general convex constraints. The second replaces the oracle by a noise-augmented randomization scheme that constructs spanning directions from the affine-hull inner normal and almost surely avoids nonsmooth boundary points when initialized outside that set. Under curvature bounds and Lipschitz continuity of the smooth component's gradient, we jointly control the spanning coefficients and feasible step lengths of the oracle construction. This yields finite-time approximate $d$-stationarity along every unit feasible direction admitting a prescribed positive step length. For both methods, we also establish a rate in the proximal directional minimization (PDM) measure, assuming uniformly bounded direction-set sizes. Randomized exploration ensures that, almost surely, every accumulation point is $d$-stationary.

infographic.key_insight: Directions kept uniformly away from the feasible-cone boundary enable finite-direction search for structured nonsmooth, nonconvex optimization over general convex sets.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework supports derivative-free optimization under nonlinear convex constraints when exact line searches and structural access to the feasible set are available.
method: Introduce η-feasible directions to overcome boundary geometry that obstructs finite search sets.
Construct search directions using either an η-direction oracle or noise-augmented randomization.
Establish approximate directional stationarity and proximal directional minimization rate guarantees under stated assumptions.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical convergence and rate guarantees, including almost-sure directional stationarity of randomized accumulation points, but no numerical benchmarks.
infographic.watch_item: Exact line searches and constraint-geometry access may be costly, and the guarantees require specific structural and regularity assumptions.
infographic.paper_title: Randomized and Oracle-Based Feasible Directions Methods for Nonsmooth Nonconvex Constrained Optimization

title: From What Is Used to What Is Missing: Rethinking Dynamic Rank in LoRA
authors: Peng Xue, Guodong Fan, Guang-Yong Chen, Xing Chen
abstract: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning with LoRA is governed by rank, which controls parameter budget and locally accessible task updates. Existing dynamic-rank methods mainly focus on capacity allocation, leaving unresolved whether the current adaptation space is sufficient for the task. We characterize the first-order information boundary of standard factor gradients, showing that their unobservable subspace coincides with the normal space of the low-rank manifold. Thus, factor gradients alone cannot distinguish under-optimization within the current space from task-relevant directions beyond its first-order reach. This motivates a geometric view of rank evolution, where tangent information optimizes existing degrees of freedom and the normal spectrum quantifies the value of new ones. Under a local quadratic model, we show that leading normal singular directions yield the locally optimal rank expansion, with spectral energy determining its gain. Building on this characterization, we propose GEAR, which turns the tangent--normal decomposition into rank evolution through tangent-space optimization, matrix-free normal-spectrum estimation for rank expansion, and task-induced geometric initialization. Across language and vision benchmarks, GEAR achieves the best average performance in all evaluated settings with substantially fewer trainable parameters. On LLaMA3-8B, it raises the average commonsense score from 86.61 to 88.45 while reducing trainable parameters from 42.0M to 14.4M.

infographic.key_insight: LoRA factor gradients cannot reveal task-relevant directions normal to the current low-rank manifold, so rank adaptation must assess what is missing—not just what is used.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Geometry-guided rank expansion can improve fine-tuning quality while reducing trainable parameter budgets.
method: Optimize existing degrees of freedom using tangent-space information.
Estimate the normal spectrum matrix-free to identify locally optimal rank-expansion directions under a quadratic model.
Use task-induced geometric initialization for the expanded adaptation space.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across evaluated language and vision settings, GEAR reports the best average performance; on LLaMA3-8B, average commonsense score rises from 86.61 to 88.45 while trainable parameters fall from 42.0M to 14.4M.
infographic.watch_item: The expansion guarantee relies on a local quadratic model, and the abstract does not quantify normal-spectrum estimation overhead.
infographic.paper_title: From What Is Used to What Is Missing: Rethinking Dynamic Rank in LoRA

title: ToroFit: Fitting Wedge Sums of Tori to High-Dimensional Data
authors: Tanishq Bhatia, Jose A. Perea, Tarek M. Zikry
abstract: Data arising in scientific applications often exhibits complex nonlinear structure. Identifying and parameterizing said nonlinearities can enable better modeling, enhance predictive analysis, data interpolation, denoising, and anomaly detection. In this paper, we develop theoretical and computational methods to detect and parametrize Euclidean point cloud data lying near a wedge sum of tori. Specifically, we use persistent cohomology and cup products to identify the distinct toroidal components, and on each component, we optimize over low-energy multivariate trigonometric polynomials for best data fit. The ensuing optimization problem reduces to generalized ridge regression, which can be solved efficiently via standard techniques. We demonstrate the utility of the proposed framework in both synthetic and real datasets, including interpolation of low frame-rate recurrent videos, attractor recovery in quasiperiodic dynamical systems, and the parametrization of gene-space cycle data for parasites and humans.

infographic.key_insight: ToroFit identifies toroidal components in high-dimensional point clouds and fits them with low-energy trigonometric models.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework provides nonlinear coordinates and fitted models that can support interpolation, denoising, and analysis of recurrent or quasiperiodic data.
method: Use persistent cohomology and cup products to identify distinct toroidal components.
Fit each component using low-energy multivariate trigonometric polynomials.
Reduce the fitting problem to generalized ridge regression.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports demonstrations on synthetic and real data, including recurrent-video interpolation, quasiperiodic attractor recovery, and parasite and human gene-space cycles.
infographic.watch_item: Applicability depends on whether the data lie near a wedge sum of tori; the abstract does not quantify robustness to noise or departures from this structure.
infographic.paper_title: ToroFit: Fitting Wedge Sums of Tori to High-Dimensional Data

title: Formalizing inverse problems in the age of AI: possibilities, pitfalls, and an invitation
authors: Christian Clason, Tapio Helin, Medet Nursultanov, Lauri Oksanen
abstract: Proof assistants such as Lean check mathematical proofs down to the axioms, and AI agents have recently made writing such proofs cheap. We describe AutoIP, a Lean library in which classical linear regularization theory, together with the functional analysis it rests on, has been autoformalized by AI agents. A machine-checked proof certifies only the formal statement it proves, so the remaining human task is to confirm that each formal statement says what was intended. We organize the library around this task: a reviewer compares the formal statements with their natural-language counterparts and never needs to read a proof. Our experience is that the risks lie in the statements rather than in the proofs, and that simple automated tests on the statements can expose problems even in the established literature. We illustrate this with a textbook theorem whose hypothesis is more restrictive than asserted. We invite the inverse problems community to extend and build on the library.

infographic.key_insight: AutoIP uses AI agents to formalize inverse-problem mathematics in Lean, shifting human review from proof steps to whether formal statements capture the intended claims.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Machine-checked regularization theory can support rigorous inverse-problem methods, but engineers must still verify that formal assumptions match their applications.
method: Autoformalize classical linear regularization theory and its functional-analysis foundations in Lean.
Organize the library for reviewers to compare formal statements with natural-language counterparts.
Apply automated statement tests to uncover problematic assumptions.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports a machine-checked library and a textbook theorem whose hypothesis is more restrictive than asserted, but provides no quantitative evaluation.
infographic.watch_item: A verified proof certifies only its formal statement; incorrect or overly restrictive assumptions can undermine its intended applicability.
infographic.paper_title: Formalizing inverse problems in the age of AI: possibilities, pitfalls, and an invitation

title: An Accelerated Proximal Gradient Method for Bures-Wasserstein Space
authors: Jakob Nylöf, Sloan Nietert, Julien Pallage, Giancarlo Ferrari-Trecate, Daniel Kuhn, John Lygeros
abstract: We study composite optimization over the Bures--Wasserstein (BW) space of Gaussian measures. Our main observation is that a useful class of BW problems can be lifted into the Euclidean space of affine transport maps, such that the lifted problems can be solved efficiently using accelerated proximal gradient methods. For objectives whose smooth and nonsmooth components admit convex smooth and convex proximable affine lifts, respectively, our algorithm BW-FISTA achieves minimax-optimal objective gap $O(k^{-2})$ after $k$ iterations. We verify these regularity conditions for potential and interaction energies together with common spectral regularizers, and we treat stochastic gradients under a suitable noise model. As a principal application, we consider Gaussian variational inference with a log-concave, log-smooth target. Here, the resulting entropy term is handled by an efficient, exact proximal step, and we improve the previous rate of $O(k^{-1})$ to $O(k^{-2})$. We numerically verify this predicted boost with synthetic experiments.

infographic.key_insight: Lifting suitable Gaussian Bures–Wasserstein optimization problems into Euclidean affine transport maps enables BW-FISTA to achieve a minimax-optimal O(k⁻²) objective gap.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For Gaussian variational inference with log-concave, log-smooth targets, BW-FISTA improves the theoretical convergence rate from O(k⁻¹) to O(k⁻²).
method: Represent Gaussian measures through affine transport maps.
Apply accelerated proximal gradients when the lifted components satisfy convexity, smoothness, and proximability conditions.
Handle the entropy term in Gaussian variational inference with an efficient, exact proximal step.
infographic.evidence_signal: Synthetic experiments numerically verify the predicted convergence improvement.
infographic.watch_item: The accelerated guarantee requires suitable convex affine lifts and does not automatically extend to arbitrary objectives or non-log-concave inference targets.
infographic.paper_title: An Accelerated Proximal Gradient Method for Bures-Wasserstein Space
